item.description:
UPDATE 4.20PM BST: Eurogamer understands that this meeting took place and the transcription is correct, with the exception of the word "revive". The transcript should read: "We will not survive if we only rely on the past."
ORIGINAL STORY 11.30AM BST: Xbox leader Asha Sharma has reportedly broadcast her intent to "create enduring new IP" alongside the company's much publicised plan to organise around its biggest gaming brands - think The Elder Scrolls, think Blizzard, etc. But according to Sharma: "We will not survive if we only revive on the past."
Sharma reportedly said this in addition to dropping more information about Xbox's next-gen console Project Helix and while reflecting on Xbox's "return to growth" after "an all-time low".
"We're backing our strongest franchises," Sharma allegedly said. "I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences."
It's a declaration which seems at odds with Xbox's recent actions. Parting ways with studios like Double Fine and Compulsion, and probably Arkane - all of which have a track record in creating new game ideas such as Keeper and South of Midnight, and Dishonored and Deathloop - seems an odd way to go about engendering a culture of courage in creation. Similarly, having an inventive studio like Obsidian work under Bethesda making a Fallout game suggests there's no immediate room there to pursue wholly original ideas. But at least Xbox is investing in Hideo Kojima's Physint, right? Right?
Cuts at id Software and consolidation elsewhere across the Xbox gaming division also reflect a company that appears to be reorganising around its biggest gaming brands rather than one intent on taking new, creative risks. Indeed, a look at Xbox's upcoming roster really only reveals InXile's Clockwork Revolution - one of its two Xbox exclusives - as an obvious contender in the 'big new idea' area. But will it be strong enough to start a lasting series?
Meanwhile, the studio behind the other Xbox exclusive, Gears of War: E-Day, fears for its future after releasing its game, despite it seeming to have been a success. That's because of the hundreds of impending cuts Microsoft still intends to make to its Xbox division. There, uncertainty looms large.
Dom reviewed Gears of War: E-Day for us recently and, generally, really enjoyed it. "Though there's still plenty of waist-high cover, ebb-and-flow firefighting, and braindead machismo, Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too," Dom wrote.

item.description:
Let's chase 'em off, Rex! Two more missiles arc toward a hapless enemy F2-A, droplets peppering my windshield as I skim past a glowering grey cloud, dulling the distant explosion. Visibility is garbage. No kidding, Tasha. The Endurance is being targeted. Uh-oh. Tonitrus Spear arriving in two minutes! They've got a high-output laser and a broad-range jammer. Sounds like a bad combo. The cockpit rattles as I climb, an insistent red flash warning me my Tomcat's icing up. But I can see the laser, and soon after the airship it's emerging from. It's in my sights. I've got this.
Wait! There are are two lasers! I have no longer got this. This is suddenly in an entirely different postcode. Even as one falls, the overlapping chatter in my ears gets busier still. Take both of them out or the carrier will take a Spear strike. Move. Don't think. Quickly now. 45 seconds. Tasha's anxious; Coster, a man of few words, knows when they're most needed: Don't panic. Stick to your training. There's a furious shudder as I swerve into another ice cloud and a missile whistles by. Arriving in 30 seconds. The music swells, the string players bowing with an urgency that suggests even they recognise things are getting desperate. 10... nine... eight... The airship finally comes into view. Seven...six...five...four... It's too late. I vainly launch one last LAAM, knowing it's not going to hit in time. Three... two... one... It's over. I slump in my seat, having spent the last few minutes perched on its very edge.
But then... Shot landed! What? A cutscene kicks in showing the last airship exploding. Joker 1, target destroyed. I instinctively leap up, and my DualSense Edge takes its maiden flight.
Wings of Theve's intense, often exhilarating, occasionally downright euphoric campaign centres on an act of propaganda. The eponymous 'Wings' is a fiction: an invention of a media guru to bolster morale during an ongoing conflict that has left people seeking symbols of hope. When your predecessor – whose own kill count hasn't even reached single figures – is downed during the prologue, you're invited to take up the mantle. It's a smart way to align you with the character you’re inhabiting: this is a series, after all, whose goal is to make you feel like a seasoned fighter pilot. Part of the brilliance of Ace Combat 8 is how it both reminds you that you're ultimately a fraud, whilst also giving you moments where you could be convinced that you're Maverick.
The Top Gun comparison has been made countless times before, of course, but it's hard to ignore the degree to which Wings of Theve owes a debt to Joseph Kosinski’s 2022 sequel, specifically. It's not just its head-on replay camera (which admittedly doesn't have the same effect as a demonstration that one of cinema most bankable stars – pre-Digger, at least – was flying a plane for real) or cutscenes that mimic some of the film's most memorable shots. Rather, it's as if Bandai Namco Aces was inspired by one of the most thrilling action movies of the 21st century: every mission feels like the most extravagant set-piece of a Hollywood summer blockbuster.
For better and worse, that carries over into everything that happens in between. One of the big differences between Wings of Theve and its forerunners is its investment in story. There's an introduction that borders on Kojima-like indulgence (which gives me enough time to wonder whether he'd have named the player character Tom-Cruiseman). The first-person interstitials never quite sold me on the wisdom of having a silent protagonist – nor, indeed, the value of its limited inputs, such as look and zoom controls and the occasional 'press X to shake hands' prompt. Yet the inherent awkwardness of the mute hero is tempered by the choice to have your precursor linger like an Obi-Wan-esque spirit. He's a combination of internal monologue and exposition device, delivering portentous lines like "the ocean sits there like an open coffin" in a whispery growl that to me sounded awfully like (apologies if this spoils the game for you) Christian Bale's Batman voice.
That adds just a hint of unintentional comedy to the game's serious-minded ruminations on war, which feel like a developer having its cake and eating it. There's much handwringing about the human cost of conflict (though the script seems to reserve greater ire for the evils of social media and how quickly and easily falsehoods can spread and take root in the gen-AI era) and it's not shy of making you aware you're a cog in both the war machine and the propaganda machine. At the same time you've no choice but to embody this role, and in effect become the pilot of legend with the improbable kill count that is inspiring the folks back home.
It's a reminder, too, that while Call of Duty and Battlefield frequently feature in uncomfortable discussions about the military-entertainment complex, Ace Combat has managed to dodge being included in these conversations like, well, a barrel-rolling MiG evading an incoming missile. Ah, but this isn't our world, Chris. This is Strangereal, not Normalreal: a place where enemy planes play dad-rock over open channels to announce their arrival, and one of your wingmen plucks out mournful guitar solos on a carrier at sundown. True, but it also features several real-world planes, unveiled with a similar reverence to which Gran Turismo affords newly-purchased cars. And – space elevators, land battleships, and colossal transports with thousand-metre wingspans notwithstanding – its scenarios feel at least somewhat plausible, not least when we're presented with haunting scenes of devastation that can't fail but evoke the kind of imagery we've seen of Gaza and Ukraine in the last few years. Wings of Theve is so overwhelming, so relentless and so stratospherically daft that for me these concerns melted away during the missions themselves; equally, it's worth spotlighting for those who might not find virtual conflict much of an escape right now.
In any case, it all makes for a surfeit of downtime in a game that is at its best when it cleaves closest to that opening quote from its 11th sortie: Move. Don't think. Quickly now. After the fact, I realise this is perhaps as close as Wings of Theve gets to a mission statement. Few series communicate a sense of urgency quite as well as Ace Combat, and if this particular entry's most arduous sorties threaten to unsettle that delicate equilibrium between exhilarating and exhausting, at its finest it delivers a rare kind of sensorial high.
What separates Ace Combat most from its immediate predecessor – and its PS2 heyday – is its focus on spectacle. Yet there's real substance beneath its visual pizzazz. Those clouds, for instance, aren't only responsible for 2026's most jaw-slackening skyboxes, nor some of its best weather effects. Visibility, after all, can be a double-edged sword, making it a key tactical consideration during dogfights. And while venturing into cloud cover can make you a little less cumulo-nimble – even reducing the range of your missile lock-on – that's all the more incentive to tinker with your pre-mission loadout.
On that front, you might be tempted to immediately splurge on new planes with better stats, but it's often more sensible to invest in parts that can extend the range and effectiveness of missiles, as well as decrease your likelihood of stalling or boost your durability. Similarly, teammate commands make a surprising amount of difference, as does your choice of plane. In missions where your attentions are torn – in other words, most of them – you can have them break formation to thin out enemy numbers, while you can instruct them to deploy special weapons, which in some cases can enhance your own capabilities or disrupt your opponents.
It's another consideration in a game that typically – and purposely – gives you too much to handle at any given time. It's not so much organised as meticulously choreographed chaos: if at times the relentless barrage of radio chatter means it's hard to divine which threats you should be prioritising, that generally feels more feature than bug. To live up to your billing, you'll need to learn to parse the vital from the incidental, and when wingman quips are vying with admonishments from other pilots, instructions and updates from various sources – not to mention noisy missile alerts to ramp up the stress – that isn't always easy.
All of which means Wings of Theve can be ever so slightly draining to play in long sessions, demanding as it is of your total attention at all times. Even in the comparatively slow-paced missions, there are developments that force you to lock in before you lock on; to lean forward and snap into focus. You're often invited to go off-piste – there's a fraught moment where you're asked to lend a hand as a rustbucket transport flies through valleys lined with anti-air ordinance. Taking those down as your wingman repeatedly shouts "MANPADS!" might, by this game's standards, seem relatively straightforward. But it suddenly turns into a frantic race against time, as a group of enemy fighters converge and you need to down them all against the clock.
That's typical of a game that never stops finding ways to up the stakes, even during the landing and refuelling sequences that otherwise offer you respite from the mayhem. You can never quite relax until the 'mission complete' text finally pops up. But the problem with so frequently upending expectations is that, over the course of 30 missions, surprises become the norm. Wings of Theve's Shyamalan-level appetite for eleventh-hour twists means that when a mission ends as anticipated, it's hard not to feel a little let down. Equally, it introduces One Last Threat – or an existing one that turns out to be still operational – once too often. If checkpoints ameliorate any frustration, some of these sorties feel distinctly less replayable as the timer ticks well beyond the half-hour mark.
Bar an early difficulty spike during an escort mission and one tedious bout of forced aerial stealth (featuring the single most misleading bit of direction I've seen in a video game for some time), the game that feels absolutely sensational in the moment. One mission's third act, where you're left to tackle an entire squadron on your own – the score hitting Hans Zimmer levels of thunderous escalation again and again – delivers a sense of giddy mastery and audiovisual splendour that could persuade even the most hardened cynic of the enduring appeal of simple power fantasies.
I figured the series' biggest online component to date would struggle to live up to the single-player. But as someone who's never been a huge competitive multiplayer guy, I was pleasantly surprised. For starters, healthy first-week sales (and a schedule that cycles between stages, with three per mode active at any time) mean matchmaking times are refreshingly short. During longer waits, or before you launch a sortie, you can have a wander around a large air base where you can spend rewards you've earned acquiring new planes, upgrading and decorating the craft already in your hangar, or perhaps even tackling a quartet of classic Namco arcade games. Costlier planes with more upgrade slots definitely give more dedicated players the edge, but as with the campaign your starter plane can hold its own – and there are some challenges you can only accomplish with lower-grade craft.
Alongside solo and team deathmatches that will prove chastening for many, the main draws are the two PvPvE modes. Co-op Warfare asks you to shoot down human and computer-controlled bogeys alike. Perform well, and you'll accrue stars, eventually being dubbed an Ace. Yet such moments of triumph don't last long, since the title effectively paints a target on your back, your opponents gaining more points if they take you down. While you can tag yourself with the D-pad to ask your allies to protect you – or else mark out an enemy ace – these commands are a better idea in theory than in practice. The pace of the game is simply too fast for these to be consistently useful; more often than not, I'd find an ally's missile already hurtling toward a target as I was about to tag it. Co-op Assault, meanwhile, sets two teams of four a common goal; there's a bit of friendly competition as Alpha and Bravo vie to be the most valuable squadron, but even low-performing players get a sense that they're contributing something to the collective effort.
That feeling is all the keener in the four-player Scrambles and eight-player Emergency Sorties, the spawning conditions for which I'm admittedly yet to fully figure out. In any case, there's a chance after a few games of Assault or Warfare that you'll hear a siren blare, whereupon you're called to take down enemy aircraft or some manner of superweapon. Yes, you're basically collectively chipping away at a colossal health bar against the clock, and there may only be three of each, but for my money these modes come closest to capturing the thrills of the campaign in a repeatable format.
There's plenty of game here, in other words – and that's not always a positive. Part of me thinks a marginally shorter, tauter campaign that excised the weakest missions and took the edit scissors to a couple more would have made it a genuine, copper-bottomed classic. Yet at its very best you could easily be convinced that Wings of Theve deserves to be described in such terms. Either way, it's a game with a laser-guided focus on giving you some of the giddiest highs you're likely to experience in a video game this year. In which case: mission accomplished.
A copy of Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve was provided for this review by Bandai Namco Entertainment.

item.title: Glen Schofield, the game-maker best known for co-creating Dead Space, has blamed Korean company Krafton - the owner of PUBG - for the shortcomings of his horror game successor The Callisto Protocol, which it published. Read more
item.description:
Glen Schofield, the game-maker best known for co-creating Dead Space, has blamed Korean company Krafton - the owner of PUBG - for the shortcomings of his horror game successor The Callisto Protocol, which it published.
In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, Schofield expressed frustrated bewilderment at Krafton's handling of his Striking Distance company, which it had invested in, during the Covid pandemic. Krafton allegedly promised Striking Distance three extra months of development time and then rescinded it.
"I was forced to ship the game," Schofield said. "I'm mad at myself, there's no doubt. I was so stunned by that decision, because we had fucking Covid. A million people died in America. I lost one of my best friends.
"Every single month, four to six people in my company were getting sick. There were times [when] our small team in Spain was shut down; it goes through a small place like that and you lose your rendering team for a while.
"The main thing you're concerned about, not that you aren't normally, is the health of your team. Making a game just became secondary because this is about life. This is about humanity."
Schofield has discussed the decision to deny the three extra months of development time before. Had it not, then The Callisto Protocol would have been released in March 2023, rather than December 2022.
This sudden rug-pull had also come after years of the studio adapting to working during a pandemic already, which Schofield said had been very hard to do.
"When you have a studio of a hundred people, you can touch a hundred people a day. When they're at home, you have to do individual calls, or I could get everybody together on Zoom," said Schofield. "But we did it. We did all these things because we were searching for the best way to do it. There were so many meetings.
"We had to learn on the job and just change everything," he added. "We got it done and everything. We saw the problems that we had. A lot of them were caused by Korean management."
Before it was embroiled in a legal battle with Subnautica 2 creators, Krafton was mostly known as the PUBG company. Having found so much success with the battle royale shooter and its off-shoots, the publisher was ready to invest in the triple-A space - but it seemingly wasn't ready for that new role.
Schofield said Krafton lacked the necessary experience to release a single-player physical game, forcing Striking Distance to build an internal team to do that. Krafton also allegedly mandated a release of The Callisto Protocol on PlayStation 4 alongside PS5, which would cost "another $20 million", Schofield said, and require sending out 200 dev kits to developers during a global chip shortage. None of that helped The Callisto Protocol's fortunes, and Krafton wasn't happy with its financial performance as a result.
"[Krafton] thought Callisto was a complete failure," Schofield revealed. "What they didn't know while all they were doing was complaining, we were doing patches. I waited until I finished all the DLC and put out 86 patches. That was a lot of fucking work. Every day you're going in, you're making changes. Some are little, others are massive. That was all to get it back to where it needed to be."
The Callisto Protocol received a mixed reception at launch, owing to technical and performance issues but also to core design elements relating to combat. In the Eurogamer review of The Callisto Protocol, Vikki Blake praised the game's production values but lamented its lack of depth and tension compared to Dead Space.

item.title: Epic Games has reportedly turned to gen-AI to finish up development on a shooter that crosses over Star Wars and Marvel, which has been internally delayed. Read more
item.description:
Epic Games has reportedly turned to gen-AI to finish up development on a shooter that crosses over Star Wars and Marvel, which has been internally delayed.
That's according to a Bloomberg report from journalist Jason Schreier, citing anonymous sources familiar with the unannounced game. Epic's in-development project - a collaboration with Disney - is said to have hit a speed bump, and the Fortnite maker is apparently telling its developers to embrace more gen-AI tools for the rest of the game's production.
The new shooter purportedly features characters from both the Marvel and Star Wars series, and the company expected to have it out the door in March 2027. Now that the crossover project has slipped, Epic reportedly told its staff to adopt an "AI first" production pipeline and finish the game with tech such as Anthropic's Claude.
In an internal message seen by Bloomberg, one game director told developers there would be "no more hand-written code" and art work should be "generated with full AI workflows" - much to the surprise of many workers.
"We're embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do," Epic's communications director, Jake Jones, said in a statement to Bloomberg.
"We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," CEO Tim Sweeney tweeted. "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal."
The Walt Disney company acquired a $1.5b stake in Epic Games a few years back, as the two entertainment giants agreed to partner on a "games and entertainment universe" somehow connected to Fortnite. There weren't any concrete details on the collaboration at the time, though the duo said players would be able to "create their own stories and experiences, express their fandom in a distinctly Disney way, and share content with each other in ways that they love". More recently, it was reported that senior Disney executives were interested in buying Epic Games outright.
Epic's push for gen-AI to infiltrate almost all levels of game development comes less than a year after it laid off over 1,000 humans. At the time, CEO Tim Sweeney told staff "we're spending significantly more than we're making, and we have to make major cuts to keep the company funded."

item.title: Developer Hello Games has somehow managed to fit its universe-sized space sim No Man's Sky onto iPhone and iPad devices, and it's partly thanks to the studio's upcoming Light No Fire. Read more
item.description:
Developer Hello Games has somehow managed to fit its universe-sized space sim No Man's Sky onto iPhone and iPad devices, and it's partly thanks to the studio's upcoming Light No Fire.
A decade after its hugely divisive launch and subsequent years-long comeback, No Man's Sky will come to IOS on the 28th of October with all of its numerous updates included. Hello Games promise the game will run on devices going as far back as the iPhone 11, and pre-orders open today.
"For nearly three years, we've had this little side project. There's something incredible about this universe fitting in your pocket," studio co-founder Sean Murray said in a deep dive video (below). "We want console quality visuals and gameplay that you can play anywhere. We support touch, we support controllers, even mouse and keyboard. This is something I've loved working on."
Murray also explained that Hello Games has made "tons of tweaks and improvements" that should benefit players on all platforms - PC, PlayStation, Switch and Xbox included. But once upon a time, the team thought a mobile port "would never be possible."
Of course, iPhones have become increasingly powerful in the decade since No Man's Sky first landed, though there's another reason why the port can even exist and run today: Light No Fire.
"We have had to think really hard about where are we going to get this performance from, and how are we going to fit in our memory profile better," Murray said while speaking to Polygon. "And some of those changes have come from Light No Fire. Things that we've been doing there where we've had to make things more performant, we're going, 'Oh, we can carry that across to all of this.' It's all one shared engine."
Light No Fire's been away from the spotlight ever since its reveal in 2023. In case you need reminding, it's a co-op adventure game set on a procedurally generated fantasy planet. While No Man's Sky aims for the stars, the studio's follow-up strips things back ever so slightly to focus on depicting one open-world planet (rather than millions) "with no boundaries" this time.
Last month, Murray suggested that Light No Fire was quite far along, but he told Eurogamer (that's us!) that he's learned a "very important lesson of not talking about things" too soon. Alright, then, keep your secrets.

item.title: Dragon Quest co-creator Yuji Horii has just released a new game that he says was made (or, rather, prompted) in about half an hour thanks to gen-AI. Read more
item.description:
Dragon Quest co-creator Yuji Horii has just released a new game that he says was made (or, rather, prompted) in about half an hour thanks to gen-AI.
In an online post from this weekend, the famed game developer recalled how he created 1983's The Portopia Serial Murder Case mostly on his lonesome. "I came up with the story myself, drew the pictures myself, did the programming myself, and created the game all by myself," Horii wrote on X.
"And now, by using AI, even if I can't draw pictures or program, I can just give instructions to the AI and create a decent game all by myself. It's truly astonishing. By the way, the production time for the game below was just about 30 minutes. Oh, and don't press the boost button," he adds, while linking to a text-based interrogation game.
その昔、PCで『ポートピア連続殺人事件』を作った時は、自分で物語を考え、絵も描いて、プログラムもして、ひとりでゲームを作りました。そして今、ＡＩを使えば、絵を描けなくても、プログラムしなくても、ＡＩに指図するだけで、ひとりで、そこそこのゲームを作れてしまいます。ホントびっくりです。ちなみに下のゲームの制作時間は、ほんの30分ほどでしたよ。あ、ブーストするボタンは押さないように。 https://t.co/slczyG52ZQ
Horii's love affair with the tech started a while ago. Earlier this year, MMO Dragon Quest 10 teamed up with Google's Gemini AI to power an NPC chatbot called "Chatty Slimey", an in-game character that can talk to players in case they're, you know, starving for human interaction in a massively multiplayer online RPG. The 72-year-old dev defended the decision in an interview with Famitsu, translated by GamesRadar, months later: "Because nowadays AI is really smart, it's fun. It doesn't matter what I ask it, it hardly ever makes things up [anymore]... It's evolving, and lately there are a lot of things you can do with it. Slimey is a conversational partner, so I think it lowers the barrier of entry to interacting with AI."
As noted by VGC, Horii is also toying with the idea of an AI-powered chatbot for one of his future games, as well. He's currently involved with Dragon Quest 12: Beyond Dreams and a surprise sequel to The Portopia Serial Murder Case decades in the making.
Generative-AI and its uses in game development have been hugely controversial in recent years - with players, developers and video game actors worried about job security. Just this month, Google and Unity revealed a quite depressing AI-game-making tool, too.

item.title: Arc Raiders has clearly managed to entice back lapsed players with its latest update, Frozen Trail, which upgrades the game to version 2.0. Many players see it as a re-launch of the popular extraction shooter, and the numbers back that up. Read more
item.description:
Arc Raiders has clearly managed to entice back lapsed players with its latest update, Frozen Trail, which upgrades the game to version 2.0. Many players see it as a re-launch of the popular extraction shooter, and the numbers back that up.
On Steam, Arc Raiders' concurrent player counts rose sharply following the update's release, shooting up to a 185,443 peak (via SteamDB). This is the highest concurrent player count Arc Raiders has seen since March, and it's notably higher than the game's usual sub-40,000 daily peaks.
Indeed, looking more closely at player numbers you can see that daily concurrents have been on a near constant decline in recent months, only bouncing briefly back up following the release of other major updates.
There is, however, a bit of caveat to these numbers: Arc Raiders launched a free trial right alongside Frozen Trail, meaning some of those players are new and may never buy a copy of the game.
Frozen Trail is a massive update, touching almost every element of Arc Raiders. It primarily adds the game's largest new map, Pendola Pass, and introduces a number of new Arc enemy units. Some other exciting additions include new weapons, a player home called The Outpost and a complete revamp of the skill tree.
The update notably also creates a new weapon meta that's intended to cater to PvE and PvP players separately, breathing life into many underused weapons and tools.
That focus on serving both of the game's audiences is perhaps why studio Embark saw fit to - finally - officially test a dedicated PvE mode. The test runs from 13th to 20th October, but there's no telling whether that's going to result in the permanent addition of a PvE-only mode.
The free trial ends today, so it'll be interesting to see whether the PvE test is enough to bring players back and keep the numbers high. A dedicated PvE mode has been one of Arc Raiders' most requested features, though, so we could see another surge.

item.description:
Valor Mortis plays a bit of a sneaky trick. For a while it keeps it straight. 'Yes', it seems to say; 'I'm definitely a Soulslike. Look at my bonfire equivalents, my healing flasks, my corpse runs, even my early impossi-boss feints. Look at my cautious action, my fog gates, the oppressive air of melancholy that lingers over these fields of mud and blood'. But jumpcut to a few hours later, and there you are: first-person wall-running, grapple-swinging, one-two parry slashing, quick-step-fire-ball-dismembering, slow-mo bullettime high-jump shotgun-blast-to-the-face-ing. This, it's fair to say, is not your usual Soulslike.
I probably shouldn't have been too surprised, of course. Valor Mortis is the work of One More Level, the studio behind the brilliant, equally frenetic parkour-and-sword series Ghostrunner. But as protagonist William Dowsett, a soldier in Napoleon's Grande Armée, wrenches his reanimated body out of the mud at the start of Valor Mortis - his comrades' corpses piled high around him on a nameless European battlefield - early signs suggest a more traditional kind of Soulslike. Admittedly, most Soulslikes don't intermittently interrupt the action so Napoleon's disembodied voice can bellow glories to the Empire directly into your brain, but the rhythms of its first-person swordplay are familiar ones.
For a while at least, your only means of offence and defence is your saber, and combat initially plays out in that classic Soulslike dance of focused observation and the patient trading of blows. You swing your sword to attack and block to limit incoming damage, a successful follow-up restoring any health that might have drained. Some enemies wield powerful, unblockable attacks, demanding a nimble sidestep to avoid; get the timing right and you're rewarded with an opportunistic slow-mo window. Defensive manoeuvres deplete your Endurance, which takes a moment to regain; quietly approaching enemies from behind opens them up to a vicious backstab. And because this is a post-Sekiro world, well-timed parries eventually break an enemy's posture, creating an opening for a powerful riposte.
It's familiar stuff, sure, but it's beautifully designed, blending weight and fluidity with satisfyingly visceral follow-ups that cap each successful encounter with gruesome decapitations and cartwheeling limbs. And the novelty doesn't wear off; there isn't a minute in Valor Mortis' 20-ish hour runtime when the fundamental thrill of swordplay falters. Even so, it's a well-rehearsed rhythm for Soulslike fans, further compounded by the ready presence of the genre's usual ticks - the bonfires (here hourglass lanterns), the healing flasks, the dropped Souls (Catalysts) that serve as easily lost currency for levelling and upgrades. But then comes the gun.
Valor Mortis' gun-blade combat set-up might suggest a touch of Bloodborne, but once you start to get a handle on things, its pace is far more furious. At any time, you can pull up your pistol and free-aim to fire without needing to slow your momentum. Headshots are good, but hit an enemy's glowing Red Plague pustule (their exact locations are randomised with every respawn so you can't get too complacent) and you'll break their defences, causing significant damage. We're not exactly in traditional FPS territory, given the relative paucity of bullets, but this extra layer of longer-range attack makes for combat with a sometimes breathless sense of fluidity. Soon enough, you'll find yourself adopting a run-gun rhythm to encounters, landing a few well-aimed approaching shots - perhaps to deal some preliminary damage or to hit rifle-wielding soldiers with an interrupt - then follow it up with some fleet-footed close-quarters swordplay.
And One More Level gracefully expands your options over time: shotguns are powerful but their long reload times are risky when an enemy is bearing down for another vicious melee strike; the two-handed rifle is useful for thinning the ranks at long range but leaves you exposed to up-close attack. Sword fans, meanwhile, can swap their starting sabre for a rapier soon enough, trading slower swings for a succession of aggressive jabs. It's also a dream for parrying, causing massive posture damage with every deflection, albeit with a catch: it can't block. That makes it a bit of a risk if you aren't confident in your timing, but I found the parry window is generous enough - and the benefits significant enough - that the rapier was my weapon of choice for the bulk of play. And actually, while I wouldn't exactly call Valor Mortis easy, it's more forgiving than you might expect, pitched closer to 'challenging' than 'egregiously punishing'.
All this and I haven't even mentioned the small but effective consumables at your disposal - grenades, molotovs, temporary ability boosts - and your Nephtoglobin-powered magic abilities (this, in case you haven't already twigged, is very much an alternative history French Revolutionary War). One transmutation turns your hand into something like a flame thrower so you can inflict burn status on enemies; another stasis-freezes them to the spot. And the Catalysts you're farming throughout can be exchanged for incremental upgrades - more health, punchier melee, and so on - even a fancy new trick. You can, for instance, unlock the ability to slow time when you draw your gun while airborne, adding even more cinema to the combat.
Together, it makes for an elegant toolkit with powerful combat potential, and it's paired with enemy design that encourages experimentation as you adapt to each one's distinctive rhythms: pitchfork-wielding villagers with erratic thrusts, super-aggressive axemen with a flurry of unblockable attacks, lanky elite soldiers with vicious claymore swings or rapid dual-wielded sabers that really test your parry timing. But as it all begins to click, it's surprising how quickly you can cut through enemies with the old headshot, dash-dodge, postule-pop, parry-posture-break trick; stately Soulslike rhythms melting away.
The first hint Valor Mortis might not be your usual Soulslike comes pretty early on, when William - needing to cross a treacherous gap teetering high on the edge of a ravine - launches himself at a jutting treebranch, swinging with all the confidence of a man raised in a circus and then landing with unexpected finesse. Before long, you're springing down ledges to reach the banks of a vast lake at the base of a Nephtoglobin-blasted railway bridge, and, from there, the parkour becomes steadily more pronounced. You'll bound across platforms, dodge incoming fire while unleashing your own devastating rounds as you close the gap, or hurl yourself off ledges to launch a powerful airborne attack. It gets even wilder later on as wallrunning and grapple swings are enthusiastically tossed into the mix, albeit only at fixed locations; and by the time you gain the ability to activate parkour points - conjuring ledges and outcrops with split-second timing to maintain your momentum - Valor Mortis feels as much like a platformer as it does a Soulslike. And levels are built to encourage this sort of play.
Progress, too, is routinely punctuated by bigger set-pieces. Some have a platform-puzzly air to them and other encounters are more enemy heavy; usually offering multiple routes around (and over) a busy confluence of patrolling mobs if you're dedicated enough to look - perhaps bypassing the encounter entirely, or offering a cheeky vantage point. Sometimes too, exploration rewards a proper boon - say, a secluded cannon you can use to thin the ranks in a particularly enemy heavy area - while small secrets and off-the-beaten track side quests provide additional reason to poke around, preventing the otherwise largely linear progress path from feeling too claustrophobic. There's even a light touch of Metroidvania to Valor Mortis' structure, and many levels include routes you can't take until you've gained the necessary abilities later on, often revealing secrets of their own - challenging fights against members of Napoleon's Garde Eternale, perhaps, rewarding skill-granting gems. And throughout it all, you're bounding and slashing and gunning with gleeful abandon.
There does come a point in the latter stages, admittedly, where Valor Mortis' action plateaus, its inventiveness wains, and it begins to show its limits - as the same relatively small selection of enemies return again and again in slightly new configurations, and you realise you're wandering around another area built from the same old shacks. Artfully disguised shacks in beautifully constructed environs, yes, but it starts to feel a little predictable.
Its story, too, never quite gets off the ground: while it can muster an evocative turn of phrase and features some strong voice acting from the handful of characters that haunt your journey, it can't quite alleviate the obviousness of it all as it dances through its "are we the baddies?" and "war is bad" motifs. And, honestly, I do kind of wish Valor Mortis wasn't quite so beholden to the all-too-familiar machinations of Souslikes. It's all here, right down to the hub world you'll revisit whenever you want to upgrade, and it's a weight that hangs a bit too heavily, holding it back from truly blossoming into something of its own.
Minor complaints aside, Valor Mortis is a delight; a gloriously entertaining Soulslike whose fluid foundational combat and cleverly designed enemy encounters would probably be enough on their own. But then One More Level goes further: the exhilarating parkour, the thrilling sense of momentum that shapes everything from the intricate level design and memorable bosses to the sword- and gunplay, elevating it further. Valor Mortis might not be your usual Soulslike, but it's a bloody good time.
A copy of Valor Mortis was provided for this review by Lyrical Games.

item.title: For many Starfield players, the need to go through a loading screen each time you want to land on a planet - rather than seamlessly travel through the planet's atmosphere like in No Man's Sky - was a big turn-off. Read more
item.description:
Now, over three years after Starfield's initial release, we're finally close to having our seamless planetary landings, all thanks to Frederik Wessberg, who's been working on a mod to enable just that.
Although the mod has not yet been released, Wessberg was confident enough in its current state to show it in a new video. The mod is inspired by Seamless Grav Jumps and Seamless Planet Takeoff -popular Starfield mods which likewise address two other pain points.
With the mod, it's now possible to enter a planet's atmosphere manually and fly in low orbit before you decide to land. The video shows the autopilot option, which lets you "leave your cockpit seat and walk freely around your ship or enjoy the views while the ship flies from orbit to ground".
The mod also seems to offer greater control on where you can land your spacecraft, including the ability to land on water. The added atmosphere is apparently made up of "real 3D layers of volumetric clouds, driven by climate data and weather systems" built from the game's data, Wessberg said.
The mod is only in development for PC at this time, and does not yet have a release target. When it's ready, you'll be able to find it and freely download it on Nexus Mods.
Developer Bethesda said prior to the game's release on PlayStation 5 that it has long-term plans for Starfield. What that means in practice remains a mystery, but a Switch 2 port looks increasingly likely.

item.title: Bill van Zyll, VP and general manager for Nintendo in Latin America, has reiterated Nintendo's stance on physical media, confirming that the company has no immediate plans to move to an 'all-digital' future. Read more
item.description:
Bill van Zyll, VP and general manager for Nintendo in Latin America, has reiterated Nintendo's stance on physical media, confirming that the company has no immediate plans to move to an 'all-digital' future.
In an interview with Youtuber Coelho no Japão, van Zyll acknowledges the interest fans have in physical media - reignited lately thanks Sony's controversial decision to announce PlayStation will be discless by 2028 - and says the company will continue to invest in physical media for the foreseeable.
"Historically, we’ve been very agnostic, right?" says van Zyll in the interview. "We go off what the consumer prefers, and take that into account very heavily. We also have a platform that was just launched. We're barely just over a year into NS2. It's got both digital and physical – that capability. There's no plans to ditch physical. We know how much the fans like it as well, so our position has been to be agnostic."
When van Zyll mentions being 'agnostic' here, he's referring to the fact that the Switch 2 ecosystem revolves around both digital versions of games - primarily purchased via the Nintendo-run eShop - and physical game cartridges that either contain full games or act as 'licenses' that allow you to play digital games when inserted. These game key-cards are not immune from controversy themselves, however: there is often consumer push-back when it turns out the physical version of a game is 'just a key card'.
Sony's decision to kill off disc-based games has been met with furore, but recently there have been signs that the company may be considering changing its mind about the move. Developers like Hideo Kojima have given their two cents about the proposition, and even CD Projekt Red has said it'd be powerless to do anything about physical media if Sony decides to stop supporting it.
So then, it's nice to see Nintendo publicly support the continued existence of games as physical media. In the current landscape, however, it's hard to predict how long it will stick to its guns on the topic.

item.title: Gears of War: E-Day's servers have been struggling because they've been suffering distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, apparently - so someone, or some people, have been deliberately trying to overload them. Read more
item.description:
Gears of War: E-Day's servers have been struggling because they've been suffering distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, apparently - so someone, or some people, have been deliberately trying to overload them.
The Gears of War community X account revealed this after a string of updates related to login issues. The account said: "Earlier today, some players experienced intermittent disconnects, login issues, or other service disruptions in Gears of War: E-Day. These issues were due to distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks targeting our online services.
"Our teams are continuing to monitor and mitigate this activity. We'll provide updates if there are any significant changes. Thank you for your patience and understanding."
The official Xbox account also tweeted: "Service for Gears of War: E-Day is back to normal. Thanks for your patience while we worked to resolve the issue." And it shared a link to track support updates related to this case.
It's a bumpy start for what has otherwise been a notable new entry in the Gears series, with Dom awarding Gears of War: E-day four stars in Eurogamer's review - it's a game of contrasts, Dom said. "Though there's still plenty of waist-high cover, ebb-and-flow firefighting, and braindead machismo, Gears E-Day proves that looking back can, indeed, help you look forward, too," Dom wrote.
This isn't the first time this year we've seen a game's online portion impacted by DDoS attacks: in January, Arc Raiders and The Finals were hit by "coordinated" DDoS attacks. Around the same time, Final Fantasy 14 was seemingly targeted by similar attacks. It's an on-going issue in games with no simple or easy resolution.

item.title: There's clearly no stopping Steam's continued growth. Valve's PC digital store and social platform set a new user concurrent record on Sunday, with a staggering 43,505,724 million users (via SteamDB). Read more
item.description:
There's clearly no stopping Steam's continued growth. Valve's PC digital store and social platform set a new user concurrent record on Sunday, with a staggering 43,505,724 million users (via SteamDB).
Yes, that's over 43 million players online at the same time across the world, both in-game and out. Incidentally, the number of players in-game also went up to more than 14 million, itself a new record.
That is the highest ever number of simultaneous users in Steam's 23-year history. It's also the second time Valve's platform has broken its own record this year, having attracted over 42 million concurrent players in January.
Steam's Autumn Sale recently ended, so it's curious the new record was set shortly afterwards and not during the sale. That said, the last few weeks have seen a number of popular game launches, most notably the worldwide release of free-to-play MMO Aion 2, which peaked at 397,905 concurrent players at launch.
Steam's list of the top ten most played games remains mostly the same outside of that, except for the big jump in Deadlock numbers (262,145 peak concurrent) off the back of a major update. Deadlock is Valve's third-person MOBA-shooter hybrid, which the developer has yet to officially announce.
These are all signs of Steam's continued expansion and its unshaken dominance over the PC space. All that user traffic, of course, translates to revenue for Valve. According to recent estimates, Valve made $15bn (~£11.10bn) from Steam by September, with Forza Horizon 6 being Steam's biggest new release so far this year by revenue.

item.title: Will de Renzy-Martin, the actor who plays lead character Coen in the English language version of The Blood of Dawnwalker, has reminded us of the value humans bring to a performance, versus AIs generating voice lines. Read more
item.description:
Will de Renzy-Martin, the actor who plays lead character Coen in the English language version of The Blood of Dawnwalker, has reminded us of the value humans bring to a performance, versus AIs generating voice lines.
Speaking in a TikTok teaser for an upcoming episode of the My Perfect Console Podcast, de Renzy-Martin highlighted how the spoken lines themselves are only half - if that - of what an actor brings. "I think the least interesting thing about what I do is the way my voice sounds," de Renzy-Martin said. "That is really all that generative AI is able to replicate.
"It's not replicating my personality and the things that I do when I'm in the room, and the choices that I make, which is all the reasons that a director or a producer would want to work with me. And there might be directors and producers who don't want to do those things [and to use AI], but then they've got to get really good at getting performances out of something - they need to have their own ideas."
The discussion reminded de Renzy-Martin of something he apparently said four or five years ago: "Actors are pretty cheap in the grand scheme of things. And if you end up with an AI that can produce the right noises, you're going to need somebody who can interact with it and get the performance that you want attached to those noises - and they're going to be much more expensive than an actor is."
The Blood of Dawnwalker project itself caused some controversy when developer Rebel Wolves revealed it had used text-to-speech AI tools while making the game in order to plan cinematics, before hiring actors to become the characters and perform the roles. Game director Konrad Tomazkiewicz has talked quite openly about potential AI use in game development as well, mostly referring to helping with laborious work such as bug fixing. Nothing in The Blood of Dawnwalker was created with AI.
Other gaming companies have taken AI's use further, such as Embark Studios, creator of The Finals and Arc Raiders, which controversially used AI to generate voice lines in both of those games.
Elsewhere, companies like Elevenlabs have established large businesses around licensing the voices of famous actors and then generating lines based upon those samples. Actor Matthew McConaughey is an investor in Elevenlabs - he who is set to appear in his first video game next year: Exodus, the Mass Effect-like sci-fi RPG. McConaughey's voice lines for Exodus have not been AI-generated, though.
Will de Renzy-Martin has appeared in a number of video games this year, including The Sinking City 2 (as Corentin de Grandemange), 007 First Light (Henry Bancroft), and Star Wars: Galactic Racer (Shade). However, it's his starring role as Coen he'll be best known for. And it's a very accomplished performance; his calm, velvety voice makes Coen a very easy and enjoyable character to be around, which is perfect for someone you spend so much time with in the game.
I awarded The Blood of Dawnwalker four stars in my Eurogamer review. "CD Projekt Red alumni create a familiar dark fantasy adventure, but one with bold and provocative ideas of its own, that's mostly, enormously successful," I wrote.

In a wide-ranging interview with GQ, which tackles topics ranging from creative burnout to the importance of 'cosy gaming', Barone also slips in some new information about what we can expect from his highly-anticipated Stardew Valley follow-up. item.description:
Stardew Valley creator Eric Barone, has given a new interview - and finally revealed a little more information about his upcoming title, Haunted Chocolatier. In a wide-ranging interview with GQ, which tackles topics ranging from creative burnout to the importance of 'cosy gaming', Barone also slips in some new information about what we can expect from his highly-anticipated Stardew Valley follow-up.
And it's all rather surprising. Per the interview, this game is a much more action-oriented affair than the cosy homesteading of Stardew Valley: "It is still what I call a town game," he told GQ, "but it's more of an action RPG - the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights."
For anyone that's played Stardew Valley, this won't be a massive shock; there is a combat element to the game, though mostly it's sequestered to one portion of the map - the mines that hold some of the game's rarest materials. If you had fun venturing in there at night to fight slimes and horde minerals, you're going to like Haunted Chocolatier, it seems. "[The new game] is for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly," said Barone.
Elsewhere, Barone noted that Haunted Chocolatier is a more "metaphysical" experience than Stardew Valley - which makes sense, I suppose, given its connection to the world of ghosts and spirits - and that "no one's playing the game until I'm ready to show it". Hence, there's still no word on a solid release date.
The last update we had on the game was all the way back in January, where Barone noted "I'm alive, the game is still in development", following up previous statements he made alluding to the fact that the world of Haunted Chocolatier is bigger than Stardew Valley. As for when it's coming out? "The bottom line is, I don’t want to give a release date," Barone said at the start of the year. "The game will come out when it's done."
If you want to learn more about the man behind one of video gaming's biggest phenomena of the past few generations, I'd urge you to read the full GQ piece: it's a sensitive, comprehensive look at a man that boasts many talents, yet is also humble and grounded. If you're interested in the musical side of his development process, I profiled Barone once in my column at The Guardian.

item.title: In yet another surprising move for Call of Duty, Modern Warfare 4 studio Infinity Ward has announced that the game's extraction shooter mode, DMZ, will be released prior to the game's official launch. DMZ will be available starting 20th October for players who pre-order a copy digitally. Read more
item.description:
In yet another surprising move for Call of Duty, Modern Warfare 4 studio Infinity Ward has announced that the game's extraction shooter mode, DMZ, will be released prior to the game's official launch. DMZ will be available starting 20th October for players who pre-order a copy digitally.
Modern Warfare 4 now effectively has three release dates. The campaign unlocks 16th October, DMZ four days later on the 20th, and the full launch - which is when multiplayer will be playable - arrives 23rd October.
Though Infinity Ward has offered campaign early access with other Modern Warfare titles in the past, doing the same for DMZ - a multiplayer mode - is certainly new. It's a potentially shrewd move, allowing DMZ to capture streamers and generate excitement about the game ahead of its release over an entire week, with a big blip every few days. It also allows players curious about DMZ to play it without feeling they ought to be making progress in multiplayer instead.
Seeing as DMZ has its own separate progression, however, players who jump in early could potentially have an advantage come launch if they manage to accrue many items, not to mention the map knowledge they would get from simply spending more time playing.
Separately, Infinity Ward hosted a Reddit Q&A focusing on DMZ, and the question of a PvE-only playlist came up. If you're unfamiliar, a recent first-look gameplay video showed an option for Single Squad Mission in DMZ, which players took to mean a mode free from other players. However, the option disappeared in a follow-up trailer, leading to confusion. So what's going on there? Infinity Ward has an explanation, albeit an unconvincing one.
"The playlist you saw is a developer playlist that was never intended to be for public use, it lets our team load into a match alone to work," the developer answered. "In the shipping game, players choose to be solo by turning off squad fill, but it's not guaranteed to be only solos in that lobby."
I'm not convinced. Though it's obviously possible for Single Squad to be a dev-only mode, they typically don't require bespoke icons. It's also curious that Infinity Ward didn't blur the image to cover that bit of it, which is commonly done in these sorts of behind-the-scenes videos of gameplay footage, whenever the camera captures something we're not supposed to see.
Modern Warfare 4 officially launches 23rd October on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2.

item.title: Phasmophobia has sold more than 30 million copies across PC and console since it launched in Early Access in 2020. Read more
item.description:
Phasmophobia has sold more than 30 million copies across PC and console since it launched in Early Access in 2020.
Developer Kinetic Games shared the milestone alongside confirming the return of Crimson Eye, its annual Halloween event, which is now live and runs until 1st November.
Crimson Eye brings blood moon weather to a rotating set of maps each day, which makes ghosts faster and drains your sanity more quickly, but pays out more in return. The event maps are Tanglewood Drive, Camp Woodwind, Grafton Farmhouse, Bleasdale Farmhouse, Point Hope (standard only), Edgefield Road, Nell's Diner, and Willow Street.
Community goals unlock the Beholder ID Card and Badge, and the Blood Moon Trophy, while personal goals unlock the Blood Moon Charm, a seasonal t-shirt, and upgrades to the Crimson Eye trophy.
If that's not quite enough for you, watch two hours' worth of Phasmophobia streams on Twitch between 8th and 15th October and you'll get a Crimson Eye t-shirt cosmetic. You can also earn double XP and rewards from 15th to 22nd October.
Ghost Hunts 4 Hearts is also back for the final week of the event, from 26th October to 1st November, in support of the American Heart Association. The Phasmophobia community raised more than $100,000 for the charity last year.
"So much has changed since I started making Phasmophobia on my own at my parents' house," said Kinetic Games CEO and Phasmophobia game director Daniel Knight.
"My initial goal was to sell 1000 units in the first year, so it's hard to believe we're celebrating 30 million. I'm so grateful to everyone who has played, and to the team who have worked alongside me on it. There is plenty more to come as we head towards 1.0."
That 1.0 release is slated for the second half of 2027, and Kinetic Games will start sharing sneak peeks of its development next year, including major overhauls to ghost design and gameplay.
The studio also launched a publishing arm, Kinetic Publishing, earlier this year. Its first game, the starship job simulator Contact Protocol, is due out in Spring 2027.
Phasmophobia is available in Early Access on Steam, PS5, PS VR2, and Xbox Series X/S. It's also coming to Nintendo Switch 2, although we still don't quite know when.
Earlier this year, Kinetic Games confirmed Phasmophobia's 1.0 launch had slipped from this year into 2027, as the studio said it was prioritising quality over speed following a rocky reception to its Player Character Update. Kinetic Games ended up apologising to players for issues with its long-awaited 'Player Character Update', admitting it "missed the mark" and "didn't deliver on our promises to you".
In numerous patches and hotfixes released since to address the many issues spawned by the latest update, the studio explained how it had been working through player feedback to provide "a much better experience for everyone playing Phasmophobia". More recently, Kinetic released Phasmophobia's second Quality of Life update, adding a raft of new Restricted maps, streamlined Evidence collection, VR fixes, and considerably more ways to die.
"We've read feedback from across the entire community. The frustration and disappointment has been clear," the team admitted.

item.title: Player Unknown's Battlegrounds is arguably one of the most important games to release in the past decade. item.description:
Player Unknown's Battlegrounds is arguably one of the most important games to release in the past decade. If H1Z1 built the foundation of the battle royale genre, PUBG certainly shaped it into the form that remains hugely successful today. We would not have seen the battle royale craze of the late 2010s without it, and millions of people around the world wouldn't know the brutal arena thrills of red loot crates, welding helmets, and the clang of steel frying pans.
Fortnite might have stolen the battle royale crown, but PUBG's name still means something even today. So when publisher Krafton announced a brand-new PUBG was in the works last month, it was an immediately exciting prospect for battle royale fans. And doubtless a daunting one for its development team, given the large shoes Ded.Net has to fill.
But what does it mean to make a new PUBG in the shadow of the original? How do you make something familiar, while keeping it fresh enough that it doesn't feel redundant? The answer may lie in Ded.Net; a grungy splatterfest being developed by Krafton's Wisconsin studio, PUBG Madison, that gives those battle royale fundamentals a more rogue-like spin. To find out more, I spoke with creative director Dave Curd about the challenges and opportunities facing the team.
"I was charged with spreading the gospel of PUBG to an audience that might not already appreciate it or like it or understand it," Curd told me at Gamescom. And that required breaking it down to its fundamentals. "What is PUBG? Is it a blue Zone? Is it the level three helmet? I think [it's] desperate survival. I think it's survival of the fittest, it's dog eat dog."
But Curd had an inkling those same themes could work equally well in a different kind of game. Which is where PUBG Ded.Net comes in. Foundationally, Dead.Net is a third-person battle royale shooter much like its predecessor. You're dropped into a map where an ever-shrinking circle forces players to fight over spoils in order to secure victory. Here, your character is a contestant in an uber violent gameshow of sorts, sending up to the pulpy action and violent media of the 90s. But Ded.Net's big twist comes in the way it draws from pick-three-style roguelites - a popular style of roguelite in which players choose their upgrades from a selection of three options - as it plays out across multiple consecutive matches.
After finishing a match, many of the power-ups and character-altering abilities you've selected can have a positive or negative impact on subsequent games. So if you, say, chop off your arms and replace them with giant blades in one match, you may have an available power-up that leans further towards melee attacks in the next one, but you could also be assigned injuries you need to work around: you might fail to reload on occasion, for instance, or find it harder to swim. Keep pushing forward into more challenging matches and you'll earn additional rewards as the risks pile up, but cashing out might prove wiser.
For Curd, the idea of introducing enticing twists for consecutive games tackles the frustration factor present in many battle royales. "You never want to go out on a loss," he explains, "but after two or three losses, you're like, all right boys, it's time to go to bed. In Ded.Net, you can still get wrecked but then, in the out-of-game, it's like 'oh my God the akimbo ability came up. I can finally dual-wield those shotguns, maybe I can play one more match'.
"That's been the theory, that chasing your fantasy of fun takes the edge off losing," he continues. "If you're trying PUBG today, you're going up against guys with potentially five to six thousand hours of play. Starting this new journey with fans together, where unfairness is baked into the experience purposefully, I don't think those wins and losses are as crushing."
However, Ded.Net isn't just an attempt to address PUBG's weaknesses; the goal is to capture its strengths too. Curd highlights PUBG's ability to organically create keystone moments - where gameplay elements coalesce into thrilling climaxes that stay in the mind long after you turn your computer off. A battle royale where you tussle for victory is one thing, but winning a match when you're a mess of upgrades and injuries is another.
Curd is keen to stress that Ded.Net isn't going as granular as other roguelites - and incremental upgrades that add five points to firing speed or stamina recharge are not welcome here. "I don't want players doing nerd shit," he says. "I don't want our players doing math. I don't want the mental load of trying to figure out how many stacks of aim-down-sight speed is optimal [...] There's never a case where my bullets hit twice as hard as your bullets. Our powers are very purposefully strategic gameplay opportunities." And a lot of them are also surprisingly out-there for a battle royale with the PUBG name on it.
Ded.Net has pulpy, grungy ultra-violence at its heart - those aforementioned sword arms, for instance, are gained by slamming your limbs into a messed-up pinball machine, and stop you from shooting guns for the rest of the match. You can also turn into a porcelain Chucky-esque living doll who jumps on allies' backs to hitch a ride. It can also hop onto enemies, occasionally giggling to warn them a tiny horror is crawling over them. And when you decide to leap in for the kill as the doll, it steals items from the player you're attacking.
According to Curd, the team has gone to great lengths to ensure these wackier gameplay elements feel meaningful rather than gimmicky. Multiple players can be a creepy doll in the same match, thanks to the inclusion of several doll-on-body attachment points. If an ally and an enemy doll is on you at the same time, there's apparently a bespoke doll fighting system.
It might sound silly, but that's sort of the point. "We're in the entertainment business," says Curd. "If you're not smiling, I'm f****** up. The whole development process when we're considering what to put in the game has been: does it make us laugh? Is it an intriguing fantasy? Do we think about it the next day? If the answers are all yes, we usually try it out."
Likewise, it's possible to hack certain objects in the game, causing all manner of mischief. A truck can be hacked to explode after a set amount of time, for instance. And speaking of trucks, Ded.Net has a dedicated seatbelt system, meaning you'll be flung through the window if you crash a car at speed without your seatbelt on. Safe drive, stay alive, kids. Ded.Net isn't the first game to do a Running-Man-style murdershow, but in a genre seemingly saturated with military simulations and family friendly cartoonishness, it's a refreshing spin on things. Does Curd think battle royales are getting stale? "It's mature," he replies. "The big boys have found their lane. But that's an opportunity. It's evolve or die out here, and I'd like to keep pushing it."
The desire is laudable, but given the prestige of the brand, I wonder if the Ded.Net team is also feeling a lot of pressure. "Pressure is a privilege," Curd says. "I'm incredibly fortunate to be in the position to be trusted with taking a swing with a very precious IP. And I think if you fixate on that, you will second-guess yourself and you will tie yourself in knots. My executive producer has been nothing but supportive; we've had a great working relationship. He told me, 'Don't worry about the numbers. Worry about pleasing the fans, worry about making something memorable.' He's interested in big swings. So I feel very supported.
"We have always developed responsibly, we believe lean teams innovate. So we're not this big huge monster that has to work or everybody is in trouble and everybody's in danger. We've thoughtfully - with the fans - incrementally been building something we think people will love."
This interview is based on a preview at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. Krafton provided flights and accommodation.

item.title: Strange Scaffold, the studio behind I Am Your Beast and El Paso, Elsewhere, has announced Gods With Badges, a narrative tactics game about the power police hold over life and death. Read more
item.description:
Strange Scaffold, the studio behind I Am Your Beast and El Paso, Elsewhere, has announced Gods With Badges, a narrative tactics game about the power police hold over life and death.
It was unveiled during the Triple-I Initiative showcase on 8th October and is due out on Steam for PC in 2027. You can check out a trailer below:
You play as Harrow McClellan, a disgraced police officer transferred back to her original post after the scandal that drove her out has become law enforcement legend. Every dialogue choice and turn-based encounter is a decision to play into that reputation or try to rise above it.
You'll patrol the open hubs of Scarhelm, a dystopian city of the future, seizing contraband, investigating complaints, and searching back alleys for evidence. Your dialogue choices, arrests, and uses of force shape Harrow's relationships with her fellow officers, the public, and the institutions around her.
Interestingly, when a situation escalates, the game shifts to isometric turn-based combat. Here you can take cover, rescue hostages, and decide how much force to use. You can also temporarily disable Harrow's body camera, unlocking new tactical and dialogue options but removing the public record of what happens next.
Gods With Badges began life as Hard Justice, an unrealised project from strategy studio Artificer. Strange Scaffold has built on its foundations and development materials, reinterpreting them in its own style.
It's also the latest entry in Project Share, an initiative Strange Scaffold pioneered last year that encourages developers to exchange technology and explore more sustainable ways to make games. The first resulted in Creepy Redneck Dinosaur Mansion 1: Re-Raptored.
"With its unique production circumstances and desire for cultural impact, Gods with Badges is among the most ambitious things Strange Scaffold has ever undertaken," said Strange Scaffold studio head Xalavier Nelson Jr.
"I'm deeply grateful to the original developers at Artificer for trusting us with their project, and can't wait for people to see what we've built on this complex, exciting foundation. We're taking it seriously - and doing something that is both intentional and striking."
The soundtrack comes from composer Kris Kirk, who also scored Space Warlord Baby Trading Simulator.
I was deeply impressed by I Am Your Beast, a prior Strange Scaffold offering. "Despite a schlocky - and shocking - presentation, [I Am Your Beast] is exactly what I needed it to be, which is a delightfully bombastic experience that neither outstays its welcome nor feels unjustly punishing," I wrote awarding it four out of five stars. "Stapled to a blisteringly powerful soundtrack, this is a trim, frenetic, thoughtful shooter that stayed with me far longer than its truncated playtime".

item.title: Arc Raiders could eventually be split into PvE and PvP modes. Read more
item.description:
Arc Raiders could eventually be split into PvE and PvP modes.
Talking to GamesRadar+ ahead of Embark's limited PvE test next week, executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said the idea of a more peaceful Arc Raiders is "possible".
"I mean, the community is already split along those lines," he said. "If the game eventually will represent that? Quite possibly. I think it's important to respect how the players want to enjoy the game, even if it doesn't necessarily fully gel with what we thought the game was initially or how we designed the game to be initially. It's possible.
"Of course, it creates some challenges on our end. We need to figure out what we really mean by that."
The test 'toggles' the option to opt into PvE matchmaking, where Raiders can't damage each other. Solos, duos, and trios will be matched into the same sessions, although Night Raids and the upcoming Frigate aren't part of the test.
Grøndal said the test, which runs from 13th to 20th October, will help Embark identify how best to implement PvE, but admitted it's "somewhat limited around some of the higher-end stuff" because it "has a chance of affecting" the overall experience.
A blog post from Embark goes into further detail, writing: "When ARC Raiders was conceived seven years ago, the vision of the game was quite different.
"We originally envisioned a raid-based PvE Co-op game with looting mechanics. While the concept showed promise, we ran into significant challenges, and eventually decided to reset the game and build the high-tension PvPvE Extraction adventure that you know today."
Embark's player data shows the split in how the community most like to play: 37 percent are friendly co-op players, 34 percent are pure PvP players, and 27 percent flit between the two. Over 70 percent of friendly players and even 40 percent of PvP players, however, have expressed a "desire for fewer hostile encounters and 51 percent of the surveyed playerbase has expressed an interest in a dedicated PvE option".
That said, there are caveats to the upcoming test, with Embark stating plainly that "it’s possible that this will not work", and the test "is not a promise that there will be a PvE mode in the future".
"But take this as an indication that we are seriously considering it," the studio added.
Earlier this week, we learned film and TV show adaptations of Arc Raiders and The Finals are in the works. Developer Embark Studios is collaborating with Chernin Entertainment to get the job done after Chernin Entertainment created the hugely successful Backrooms horror film.

item.title: Silent Hill producer Motoi Okamoto says Konami is looking at "a number of projects" after the first wave of new Silent Hill games. Read more
item.description:
Silent Hill producer Motoi Okamoto says Konami is looking at "a number of projects" after the first wave of new Silent Hill games.
Talking to Famitsu, Okamoto said Konami was already thinking about what comes after its first run of new Silent Hill games, teasing "second and third waves" of releases.
"All three titles we initially announced were able to be released successfully, so we're relieved (laughs)," he noted. "They've also received high praise, and we are satisfied with it.
"Successfully launching this 'first wave' comes with great relief, but we're not stopping here; we must think of the second and third waves. We can't share specific details, but we're currently looking at a number of projects."
Interesting, Okamoto also hinted that it had taken some time to convince Konami execs, stressing that "one remake is not enough".
"As a producer, I cannot let it end only with that," he said. "If there were only one release, wouldn't people think that the development is going to be cancelled again, I thought."
Silent Hill: Townfall is out now. We awarded it four out of five stars in Eurogamer's Silent Hill: Townfall review, writing: "Silent Hill: Townfall is, though, an often phenomenal ride; reverent to its roots, rich with ideas, and yes, properly unnerving too. And there is, I think, some pleasing symmetry in the fact the two grandaddies of the survival horror genre - Resident Evil and Silent Hill - have bookended the year with their own distinctive highs; one with a warm eye to the past, the other taking bolder, more experimental strides".
Silent Hill was resuscitated with a bang in 2022 when Konami announced Silent Hill 2 Remake, Silent Hill f, Silent Hill: Townfall, Silent Hill Ascension, and movie Return to Silent Hill all at once, with Silent Hill: The Short Message shadowdropped thereafter, too. Series producer Motoi Okamoto said that the key to the franchise's revival was to "cherish" a "strong psychological horror narrative".
"As long as that remains intact, we feel that we can be more liberal and experimental with what kind of gameplay we take," Okamoto said at the time. "So I think that's very evident in how Silent Hill 2, last year's Silent Hill f and, of course, Silent Hill: Townfall, are all very different gameplay experiences. We feel that as long as we keep the narrative core intact, there's very much room to keep the gameplay style changing."
Don't forget, Bloober Team - the studio behind the Silent Hill 2 remake - is now working on a remake of the original Silent Hill, which Konami announced in June 2025.

Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Dom enjoys being back in Gears of War, which they should with a name like that; and Bertie ekes every last drop he can get out of The Blood of Dawnwalker before saving his family.
But enough of that: what have you been playing this week?
And don't forget we have an entire dusty archive of previous What We've Been Playings, just in case you don't trust your memory any more and want to check which games you've played, and see what you thought of them.
God, Horde Siege is good. Initially, I thought it was a bit too contrived compared to the very simple past version of the mode, that many people come to Gears for in the first place. But the open-ended maps, potential for cross-squad interplay and emergent moments... It's pure video game popcorn movie stuff. I assumed I'd play Gears for review then put it down, but with Siege... it's a good job there are no other big games coming out soon. Right? Right?!
I've got one day left before Brencis' coronation! In other words, I've got one day left to save my family before he presumably eats them as part of his dastardly plan to take over the world. To catch you up: I've already finished the game but I reloaded a save so I could see more of the world. And I've been stretching it out, trying to push into as many nooks and crannies as possible to see what else is out there.
I'm glad I have. I'm constantly impressed with this game. I most recently got close to one of Brencis' vampire-gang people Xanthe, the veiled kind of witchy vampire, and learnt more about her backstory and what she's been, um, working on in her spare time. And like so much else in the game: there's real genuine storytelling value in what you find. Creepy, twisted, but also heartfelt. Suffice to say I made a deal with her because she's awful. Let's see what happens.
I've been playing Quake 3 again... in a browser. I know this isn't a particularly shocking revelation given that Quake Live, I think it was, did the same thing. But the version I was playing today was recompiled by AI - I was testing it for a news story. I wasn't smiling while playing it I promise!
I had meant to only play for five minutes but I soon found myself at the top of the scoreboard - me! - and couldn't pull myself away. It was carnage; there were way more people than the map could handle so people were spawning on top of each other and gauntlet-punching each other to death more often than not. But it was a reminder - AI aside - of how enticing this game is, especially when there are a lot of people playing it.
